comments.body: Capital punishment was a popular topic for high school juniors writing 4-6-page persuasive research papers. I probably read about a hundred of them over twenty-five years—thus I might be out of date about many things, but I am well-informed about this. The better essays were able to identify several reasons to use capital punishment: deterrence, negotiating room before trial, money saved not keeping criminals in cages, punishment for an egregious crime, offering the victim's family closure or revenge. However, studies prove that the existence of capital punishment doesn't deter murderers and it generally costs millions to execute someone. It is possible to offer taking the death penalty "off the table" as a plea deal. As punishment it is certainly cruel, and in too many cases both cruel and unusually torturous. While some loved ones are grateful for closure, others suffer the same moral quandary that society does as a whole. The strongest opposing argument is that most of us and the rest of the world feel capital punishment is a mistake. We also make mistakes about who we kill; a study some years ago estimated that approximately 6% of those executed were innocent of the crime that cost them their life. Few would agree with a student who acknowledged that statistic but explained, "That's the price of living in America." Most Americans don't support deliberately killing anyone, even when we believe they "deserve" to die.

I have a 22 month old grandson. He has the same number of neurons as I do (about 86 billion with at least a hundred trillion synapses.  22 months ago all those neurons were just busy perceiving his new environment and reacting to stimuli.  There was no self awareness, no intention, no consciousness.  He was a meatloaf with needs.  We loved him of course but there wasn’t yet a “him”. 
Fast forward 22 months. J. Said his first complex 7 word sentence. 

“I go play shapes now, bye bye!”  There was an “I” separate from his astonished parents.  There was the intention (still an abstraction) to do something in the future that he wasn’t currently doing. There was the memory of having done it before and taken pleasure from it.  There was the awareness of time (now). There was the awareness that his intention and his future action were unfolding within the context of a social network and needed to be greased with appropriate social cues (bye, bye)
In December 2024 there was just a really complex biological computer running trillions of computations searching and finding connections.  

In October of 2026 there is a self-aware center of consciousness that calls itself “I” , makes plans and locates them in time and transforms them into actions all within a web of social connections that require their own vocabulary and categories in order to manage.  

Let’s be a little humble when we talk about what AI is and what it isn’t and what might become 3 months from now.  

We don’t know jack

Growing up in Canada, the legal drinking age is 18 or19, depending on the province. We also normalize casual drinking at a younger age. At my prom, we had parents who held the afterparty at their farm house (outdoors). they knew kids were going to drink, but they wanted to be there if anything bad happened (they watched from the balcony). 

When I moved to the US, one big cultural difference was apparent - the desire to go on college benders was "rebellious", "exciting", etc. There were so many teen movies in the 90s that really glorified underage drinking, and getting "blackout" drunk. I think we really need to have more open discussions, earlier, with our kids, and they need to be comfortable telling us what they're up to. We can only love and guide with as much as visibility and understanding we have.

In law school you learn that “hard cases make bad law”, which means that cases like this one risk being decided with an appeal to emotion rather than through careful consideration of the facts.  That is unfortunate — and I say this as a feminist and a lawyer with nearly four decades of courtroom experience — for all who believe in the rule of law. 

Those of us who have tried criminal cases know this one  overflows with evidentiary problems, not least is that the complainant has admitted she was very drunk and high from using a drug that produces dissociative effects. The law requires the prosecution to prove beyond a reasonable doub that the complainant clearly did not consent to sexual contact with those beyond the initial group.  Any defense lawyer worth their law license will cross-examine the complainant about her alcohol and ketamine use on that night — not to show she was asking for trouble, but to show that her memories of non-consent or having her will over-borne are unreliable. Defense counsel will follow with expert testimony about how alcohol and ketamine individually and together impair memory and can result in false memories. These defense will credibly argue to the jury that the complainant’s impairment on its own constitutes a reasonable doubt.  

I fear sexual assault, like every woman I know, and wish to be safe in this society, but the lessons offered by this case are not the ones most commenters here think they are.

comments.name: Dave

I think there will have to be a lot of conversation about what consent means, how it can be revoked, and how substance intoxication alters consent.  Two points: NY has this "voluntary intoxication" statute, whereby if you willing ingested (or snorted) a substance that you know could cause you to lose decision making capacity, it apparently doesn't matter if you took that substance when you had capacity.  

Second, and perhaps underappreciated, ketamine is a disssociative anesthetic.  It causes people to have out of body experiences and I would argue likely diminishes or eliminates logical decison-making in many cases, but doesn't necessarily cause people the same level of (obvious) impairment that severe alcohol intoxication generally would.  Thus, when several other men (not part of the now notorious 7) peered into the room and she was apparently speaking coherently and perhaps even stating she was "good", it's not like she necessarily wasn't severely impaired at that point.  There is significant movement to repeal the voluntary intoxication statute, though it won't matter for this victim.  But perhaps this terrible episode will force a national reckoning on Greek life, substance abuse, and sexual assault in higher education.  One can only hope.

comments.name: Grant
comments.body:
The case is, of course, an extreme manifestation of gendered issues within our society.

But it comes down to what rights do we want to protect, and what responsibilities are we willing to accept in order to have those rights.

And in this case, on one side, the rights that were protected were the right to get drunk (to have 10 drinks in 3 hours after having been illegally served in a bar), the right to accept alcohol and drugs from someone who offered them to you, the right to have sex when you’re drunk and on drugs. 

And on the other side, the right to have sex with someone who is drunk and on drugs, who might not be making good decisions for themselves, who despite actively engaging in sex, might not be capable of active consent. 

But the tradeoff is that there are responsibilities that we have in order to have those rights. We have the responsibility to not put ourselves in positions where we might regret having sex in our drunken drugged state. We have the responsibility to say no I don’t want that 10th drink, no I don’t want those drugs. We have the responsibility to not have sex if consent is actively denied. (And obviously, if consent is denied or withdrawn, it’s rape.)

I would prefer we put the responsibility on people to require active consent regardless of someone else’s state, as is the law elsewhere.

But that shifts the responsibility to protect your own self-interest from what this law said, from you to someone else. And that would be ok with me.

Rape allegations should always be taken seriously.  However, this is a terrible case to use as evidence that the justice system is broken.  The system functioned appropriately.  The district attorney did not receive a rape allegation. I'm sure he would have acted differently if he had. 
The real question here is whether the Cornell police intentionally omitted the word rape from their report or pressured Jane Doe to omit it. The fact that Jane Doe made multiple corrections and edits to their summary document and did not include a rape allegation implies it was not her intention to do so, and carries great evidentiary weight.
Much is being made of the varying and changing accounts by participants.  Of course they vary: By self-admission, they were all  consensually drunk and high on K and having sex with multiple partners.  What could go wrong?
It is also highly significant that the rape allegation came after "the whole campus knew" because of social media.
None of us knows what actually happened. The participants were severely impaired and it is evident that even they don't know for sure exactly what happened and if/when some line of consent was crossed. But to come back later, after a night of monumentally poor and irresponsible decision making and claim rape, well, "The lady doth protest too much, methinks."

But crimes appear to have been committed, informed consent was not obtained by males 3 thru 7 (or whatever) and she's the victim. They should be held legally accountable. 

But everything I've read suggests it will be nigh impossible to convict them. Good things will come of the publicity around this sordid and depressing story, just as good things came out of exposing Harvey Weinstein, but on college campuses where kids get drunk and hook up, these kind of tragedies will continue to happen, and colleges and universities will continue to try to minimize them and protect their reputations.

I recall Jodie Foster's movie The Accused, and the storm that created in the late 80s. I think a major plot point was the focus on those who watched the rape and didn't attempt to stop it. They got their comeuppance in the movie, but the Chi Phi fraternity members who stood by won't get their comeuppance now.

comments.name: Michael
comments.body:
In addition to my comment on the previous post, I wanted to share my own experiences:

I was in a relationship in college which, by most people’s standards, would be considered somewhat abusive both physically and psychologically. I eventually tried to forgive my ex girlfriend, and never ended up reporting her to any authorities. I shared my experiences with a school psychologist, who provided great emotional support, but never once suggested that I reach out to Title IX or law enforcement. By contrast, multiple female friends of mine were redirected by school therapists to these resources for objectively less severe concerns.

For the record, I do not consider myself to be a rape victim. By some standards being circulated online, my ex-girlfriend would be a rapist, but as mentioned above I find these to be ridiculous. I may be a victim of beating and    manipulation, but the (not directly related) sexual misconduct on her part was misconduct, not rape.

One of my friends from high school, however, was actually drugged and raped by two girls in college. Despite his attempts to seek justice the two ladies got off scot-free and he was ridiculed and humiliated on campus, even by some of his own “friends” for reaching out. Can you imagine how emasculating and degrading it is even in today’s culture to claim that you were raped as a man, esp. by two women? This is why I believe it’s important to support *victims* in general, and not only to make the discussion a gendered one.

comments.name: Query
comments.body: This is awful situation and I feel terrible for the woman involved, and some of the men as well. But the reporting is indeed bizarre. The NYT published a story yesterday saying the police failed to pass to the prosecutor "her unequivocal statement that she had been raped." But in the same story it describes the statement as: "I don’t remember the very end of the event where I was raped,” she told them. “I can say with 100 percent confidence I was raped." It is inconsistent statement, and clearly not unequivocal. The stories also repeatedly say she was "plied" with alcohol and drugs, when they really mean to say she was offered and accepted drugs, seemingly like everyone else at this party.  There was poor behavior all around here, and the timing and equivocations don't help from a legal perspective, and the reporting on this is both confusing and clearly seeking to tell a sensational story in a certain way. There are important takeaways here about what the law "should" say, and about what constitutes consent and what does not. But the reporting fails to delve into this topics meaningfully, and worse, has painted prosecutors as failing when in fact bring a weak case and losing (and the standard remains, "beyond a reasonable doubt") would be bad for everyone.

comments.name: Kevin

The A.I. capital investment boom's effect on the economy and the course it will likely take, can be compared to the history of the Japan bubble effect in Hawaii. In the late ‘80s the exchange rate was deliberately manipulated to increase the value of Yen relative to other currencies. Japan’s then-successful companies had excess capital reserves. Banks offered loans against assets to companies and individuals at near-zero cost. All were encouraged to invest internationally. Hawaii experienced an influx of capital, with companies concentrated on building lavish resort hotels and housing. During the land-acquisition and construction boom, the broader Hawaii economy boomed too. Capacity soon outstripped demand from hotel guests, even while Japanese tourist numbers were high. When the wider Japanese bubble burst, Japanese tourist numbers collapsed. Hawaii’s resort industry worked through overcapacity in hotel and resort housing for a decade. 

Tech companies have the capital, and investment in infrastructure is juicing the economy, but once capacity is built out, there will not be enough demand to support the capex. Demand will lag initially because, while A.I. is fast, human adaptation is slow. When revenues fail to meet capital-return goals. The decline in these enterprises' valuations, combined with the drop in capital investment in infrastructure, will collapse the wider economy. A lot of  A.I. suites will  be empty.

I was a grad student at Cornell in the 1980's and taught a number of freshman. Here's what makes Cornell different from other institutions:

1) The institution and many of its students and faculty are oddly insecure and work hard to prove themselves. Because it is partially a state institution and partially a private institution, it is the easiest Ivy league school to gain entry to. The "weed out" curriculum and culture put extra pressure on students to excel.

2) Cornell does not offer its students many healthy ways to deal with its stress. Ithaca, NY, is geographically isolated, has difficult weather, and challenging (if beautiful) terrain. So undergrads turn to reliable forms of release: alcohol, sex, and drugs. Binge drinking (beginning on Thursday night) was popular among undergrads when I was there. These habits create circumstances where date rapes/sexual assaults can occur. 

3) Cornell has long had problems addressing student mental health issues, sometimes contributing to student suicides. (In the 1980's, my students would talk about "gorging out.") As a parent or a student considering Cornell, I would think about what this current case reveals about the institution's culture and how it deals with vulnerable students. Trauma victims, such as Jane Doe, need support, which Cornell is unlikely to provide. 

So, attend Cornell at your own risk.

I moved to New Zealand about twenty years ago and live about five minutes north of a Queen Elizabeth protected wetland, across a small highway from a Queen Elizabeth protected woodland.

Recently all the farmland (about 11km of rolling green hills) between our town and the one to the south has been sold to property developers, and with the decision of a single National Party minister it's all been rezoned as residential for about 7000 homes under a Fast Track procedure allowing projects to proceed without the normal requirements for environment, traffic management, infrastructure, schools, parks, etc. 

With the national elections coming in a few months, these developers are moving as fast as possible to flatten and terrace hillsides, get as much done prior to the elections, when there is the possibility of a different government and a different minister making a different decision. But if the National Party regains control this will all proceed. 

That a single minister can determine the fate of an entire valley in a country that pretends to be Clean and Green seems like something that needs to be changed. But it's a small country and the people with money make all the decisions here. Our town is trying to organise but we're 1500 people against a project that's worth hundreds of millions. I suppose it's just a smaller scale situation to what happens in North America.

People in the Governors office -- or people reading this article -- have no idea what actually happened here. This is to say, broad statements about how this particular case calls us to examine how trauma impacts young women, or should cause us to reexamine our current laws, are premature. 

From the information that can be parsed together from the articles that have appeared, it is entirely possible this was an adventurous woman testing boundaries (and maybe making life mistakes at the age many of us do) that was subsequently convinced by well meaning friends and family that she was a victim.   The way this narrative has stolen her agency is just a little shocking and somewhat antiquated.  Obviously, once a suit is filed, you make the most black-and-white case you can, but none of that obviates the possibility that this women is now locked in this position by her inner circle and, now, political circumstance.

Which brings us back to the governor's involvement and the nationalization of this opaque episode.  The public will never know what happened here as it's doubtful any of the players will ever clearly remember.   That makes the nationalization and politicization of this affair reckless and somewhat self serving for the politicians and media.

I’m so glad that the NYT ran this article; the details could really help other leakers be diagnosed more quickly. Based on my own experience with a leak and learning more about the topic, I’ll add the following:

•	Not all leaks cause the classic positional headache described in this article. Sometimes the symptoms are more general: non-positional headaches, fatigue, dizziness, vision issues, etc. Brain sagging can cause a wide range of symptoms.
•	Imaging ability has been improving in recent years, and some specialists can do better and more detailed imaging than others.
•	Leaks in the spinal area are more common than ones in the cranium, and the diagnostic and treatment processes are different for each. Anyone suspecting a leak would do well to read up on the differences between the two.
•	Leaks aren’t extremely rare! According to the Spinal CSF Leak Foundation website, a great resource, spontaneous spinal leaks are uncommon but not rare.

Finally, IMO there’s no rational excuse for having a system where practitioners who work in neurology or with headache patients don’t recognize a positional headache as a classic symptom of a leak. It isn’t just an issue of NPs and PAs not knowing—many leak patients report that their neurologists have a seriously outdated or inaccurate understanding of leaks. It’s pretty common for leak patients to go years before their leak is diagnosed (and again, leaks aren’t actually that rare).

My wife, a flight nurse, suffered from a postural headache for over two years that severely impacted her life. She had numerous visits to neurologists at several famous university hospitals, went though numerous diagnostic procedures, including having blood injected into her spinal canal in order to patch the leak. None of the procedures worked. But one day she got up and the headache was gone. Since then not a day goes by that she's not grateful or appreciative of the absence of her headache.  
Finding the source of the leak isn't as easy as the article makes it out to be. Many people suffering from spinal fluid leaks never have the exact location diagnosed in spite of MRI's, etc. and this is not because of incompetence or laziness on the part of medical professionals, as many readers of this article imply. The issue isn't so much diagnosing the cause but rather finding where the fluid is leaking from.  Thank you, Dr. Sanders, for highlighting this terrible affliction which is much more common than one would think.

comments.name: George Bohmfalk
comments.body: An a neurosurgeon who saw many patients with CSF leaks, the description of positional headaches made this my first suspicion. They can be the devil to track down and surgery to seal them often fails. Often the leak is just above the nasal cavity and either presents as a constant runny nose, often misdiagnosed and allergy or sinusitis, or is not noticed as the patient simply swallows the constantly leaking fluid. Several of my patients presented with meningitis, as there's always a risk of infection with fluid leaking out. I'm sorry the initial neurosurgery PA missed this. This patient had nothing to suggest migraine, aneurysm, or many other possibilities. This was a CSF leak until proven otherwise. Glad it eventually turned out well for her.

I’m all for working to slow down global heating. 

But articles like this do not address the full portfolio of products that are produced from crude oil (oil) that drive the wealthy world’s standard of living. Oil is distilled to give us asphalt, roofing tar, lubrication oils, diesel fuel, gasoline, kerosene (jet fuel), heating oil, light gases like propane, butane, ethane (from which we derive plastics that are ubiquitous in our world), and sulfur for fertilizer among others. 

In other words, the products that drive and uphold our material standard of living here in the wealthy world. 

Renewable electrification of transportation and providing residential electricity are very important, but renewable energy cannot drive the heavy lifting (bulk transportation, mining for materials for renewables, industrial steam, etc.) that enables our overall high standard of living. A standard of living only available to a fraction of the global population.

To bring this into clearer focus, a barrel of crude oil does about five years of one human's work, all for an initial investment in the barrel of oil of around $90 to $100 today.

So, the only question that matters, one that is never asked is: “Who in the wealthy world is willing to lower their standard of living to fight global heating while allowing the unwealthy world to gain a better standard of living while we work to lower the global heating we are now committed to, much less prevent much worse outcomes?”.

Who goes first?

MB

Converting Germany's grid from coal and nuclear requires at least three new long distance, high tension power lines from North Sea offshore wind turbines to southern Germany.  They are to this day not finished due to NIMBY opposition in southern Germany, particularly Bavaria. Reliance on intermittent solar power makes for difficult electricty grid management, as demonstrated by recent the widespread outage in Spain.  I recently saw a letter to the editor of the Financial Times of London from a learned reader stating the conversion to renewables in Britain would always mean higher electricity costs because the necessity for much more back-up (fossil-fueled) facilities, than under a fossil-fuel based system.  Particularly galling was the 1990 electorally determined (bad polling in an impending state election in southwest Germany just after Fukushima) decision by Merkel to shutdown Germany's 4 remaining nuclear plants ahead of schedule without telling the voters the full cost and risks (more Russian gas) of losing 10% of Germany's electricity generating capacity. It is not possible to consider and discuss climate without first knowing what causes temperatures to rise and fall as a result of daily rotation. It is not possible to consider climate without first explaining what causes global temperature rises and falls as the Earth rotates daily and orbits our parent star. Until those two cycles are accurately described as a starting point for planetary climate, humanity is being unnecessarily subjected to undue guilt by people who can't describe what causes the daily cycle, including organisations like NASA.

"As Earth orbits the Sun, it completes one rotation every 23.9 hours." NASA.

" It is a fact not generally known that, owing to the difference between solar and sidereal time, the Earth rotates upon its axis once more often than there are [24-hour] days in the year", NASA.

A combination of tones played over the PA and subtle flashing lights would be the cue to carefully search for an explosive device.

Back in those days the side streets, like most of London, contained a plethora of small Italian and Jewish owned cafés where one could get an excellent coffee something good to eat, ranging from bagels through to "English breakfast"; every café its own unique experience usually run directly by the owners. 
Today virtually all of them have gone, replaced by the ubiquitous green and white logo offering sugary beverages in a clinical, mass produced atmosphere.

comments.name: Peter
comments.body: The days of private cars “whizzing”  down Oxford Street have long gone. A thicket of traffic regulations has seen to that.

comments.name: LS
comments.body:
Lyons Corner House. Lunch or afternoon tea. 50s and early 60s. We always dressed up. Often wore our little white lace gloves. The sugar came in cubes, and it was a treat to suck one or two. By the 70s l was there every day taking the Northern Line (mostly) from Edgware to Bond Street Station where l worked close by. Selfridges and then Miss Selfridge was the best place to shop. Oh and yes, l was there during one of those Irish bomb scares. But Christmas was always the best - the lights and storefronts looked so beautiful. 
Memories long forgotten - but thanks for this time travelogue - a wonderful reminder of good times long gone.

comments.name: Lawrence

comments.name: Ma Co
comments.body:
I live in London and Oxford Street is one of the areas I avoid at all costs, mainly because of the lack of pavement for the quantity of shoppers.

Private vehicles are not needed in London and those who choose to drive lowers the quality of life for everyone else. Those who want to drive in the UK can do so at nearly every other car- centric city in the country. The street should have been made car free decades ago.

comments.name: Ian
comments.body: As an Aussie living in Soho, London, the delights of Oxford Street are just a few minutes walk away.  From Tottenham Court Road to Marble Arch there’s so much to see and just wandering along and taking it all in is a pleasure.  For anyone visiting London it’s a must see.  Soon the Christmas lights will be up in Oxford and Regent Streets, a magical sight.

Want to get them exempted, and secure funding from your district?

Define them as "athletic equipment."  Put it under the Football line in the budget.

comments.name: Dan Freudenberger
comments.body: My dad, though not usually a fan of cliches, used to say "Teach a boy to blow a horn and he'll never blow a safe." I took up the trombone and learned the discipline of daily practice so I could hit high B-flat. Two memories of fantastic music teachers like those quoted in this article will always stay with me. One teacher (who had played in a U.S. Navy band conducted by Sousa) told me after a lesson that I was a real trombonist. My high school band/orchestra leader played sousaphone in our football marching band because we would otherwise lack a tuba player to help us stay in step. Great teachers stay with you forever. Ill-advised tariffs on brass do not rank up there with, say, adulation of Putin, but bravo to the Times for this article.

comments.name: mbl14
comments.body: I played the cello 20 years ago for 8 years (highschool/college) and the price was that high then. Never did own one, always rented.

comments.name: ARL
comments.body: Perhaps the Music Dept Chair could point out the Band and Choir teacher:student ratio is even more favorable to the district than the 50 person gym class or the Computer Lab or a study hall. Or is it time for Districts to go to half days with students on shifts, as they did in the 80s.

comments.name: MR
comments.body:
Runaway inflation has eaten into the things that matter most. While wages and bank balances look high on paper, ordinary people can no longer easily spend on ordinary things that bring joy. 

Many years ago I lived splendidly on a PhD stipend, my children lacked nothing. Music lessons, sports training, summer camps, a ski trip. Today, in my peak earning years, I am grateful that my children are all grown up, we would not be able to give them all those opportunities so easily.

comments.name: Scott
comments.body: This is an ancillary effect of attacks on the humanities. Culture considered broadly is considered by America's leaders -- from the national to the local level -- less important than STEM so they do not invest in it. In Texas, our HS football stadiums are like palaces, but music programming still faces budget cuts.

comments.name: MFHB
comments.body:
This is the economic reality of music. 

Once 12 people with drums, brass instruments, and a mic'd singer could be louder than an orchestra, big band took off and orchestras started waning because 12 people playing metal instruments is cheaper than 70 people playing handcrafted masterpieces. 

Then amps and solid-body guitars came about and rock, blues, and bee-bop reigned supreme because four people playing factory-made instruments is cheaper than 12 playing brass instruments.

And now digital music is replacing rock because one person with an iPad is cheaper than four people with instruments. 

It's a bummer for the kids, because there is something to be gained from mastering a physical instrument and learning to play as a group.

comments.name: Henry
comments.body: The professional musician pipeline will likely remain unscathed from this. There's often so much privilege in a household when most professional musician pathways are first built as children. But without introducing the joy of music and performance to young people and humanity's musical history, we're going to see a new generation of people who may lack the ability to tell the difference between AI and human made music and the final nail in the coffin for music patronage.

articles.title: Soaring Instrument Prices Could Stop the Music at Many Schools
articles.summary: When a single cello can cost $1,000 and a tuba $9,000, tariffs are straining meager band and orchestra budgets.

comments.name: CC
comments.body: Lovely, if selective, background. It would have been interesting for Fabricant to consider the extent to which her evident wealth paved the way. The women's movement cannot advance without honest consideration of the role of material advantage-- and the implications for women who lack such resources.

comments.name: Dimitroula
comments.body: What a delightful piece. A potent reminder of reading her byline ages ago, when fresh, local food was merely enjoyed for what it was -- long before the advent of "foodies" in the '90s, followed by overwrought restaurants and chefs preparing overwrought dishes, then appearing on TV in myriad cooking shows and baking contests.

comments.name: Warren Bobrow
comments.body:
Andy Smith the celebrated writer and editor (and teacher)... asked his class on Food Writing at the New School in NYC, if anyone knew who Clementine Paddleford was.  

What he received was a room of blank stares.... 
(I took the class, so I know what was said...) 

Ms. Paddleford was the first food journalist who made it possible for food writing to even exist during her time, way before the modern era of food writing.

comments.name: AJ
comments.body: Good  story of a pioneer’s beginnings. We all appreciate farm to table food. But truly , even for families with a reasonable income , good ingredients in the current climate are unaffordable. A box of strawberries  for $9.99? What is the needed  annual income to maintain a farm to table style?

comments.name: Lorraine Fina Stevenski
comments.body: Those were great days of finding recipes in the NY Times that were delicious and were worth saving. Real food writers and REAL food in those early days at the NY Times. My Mom saved many recipes she pulled out of the NYT magazine. It was a simple time when food was delicious and great ingredients were easy to find. We didn't have to worry about our food supply being poisoned by chemicals, bacteria or artificial ingredients. There was no organic food then because most everything was grown or raised organically. Now so many food writers try to impress with quirky mismatches of ingredients and really badly written recipes.

comments.name: Cal Hancock
comments.body: FloFab is the best.  I remember her review in the Times back in the early 2000's of my Maine company's award-winning Lobster Mac & Cheese.  She had sampled it at the Fancy Food Show and described it this way - "this everyday food assumes cashmere quality comfort.”  We used that quote over and over to market our products.  It was epic.

comments.name: Annette
comments.body: My mother, who died 35 years ago, was a huge fan of Florence Fabricant. She was always passing on tips and recipes from Mrs. Fabricant when I was a young newlywed (who didn't pay much attention). Now I  understand why! They both had the same passion for fresh seasonal produce and fish, and over the years I've developed the same, much to the amusement of my family. I will have to read Mrs. Fabricant's memoir. If Mom were still here, I know one of the things that would be on her Christmas list ...

comments.name: Jim
comments.body: Can't wait to read the memoir!  I have been enjoying Ms. Fabricant's columns for many years and have learned much from her.  The NYT has, hands down, the very best food and restaurant writers in the country.

articles.title: I’ve Been Writing About Food for 50 Years. Here’s How It Began.
articles.summary: In this excerpt from Florence Fabricant’s new memoir, “Salty, Not Sweet,” she recalls how she wound up writing for The New York Times.

comments.name: john
comments.body: A companion book would be "Hands on the Plow"  a book reminiscences from SNCC women who were in the forefront of the Southern Freedom Movement.

comments.name: Satori
comments.body: Simple formula for a best selling book: (1) write the "unsung story," (2) about the women behind, (3) some historic event, invention, or great accomplishment.  Oh yes - and the author's name must be female (preferably of a distinct minority or ethnicity).   A surefire NYT top 10.

comments.name: SRMT
comments.body: This book is very welcome.

comments.name: David Breitkopf
comments.body: Joan Baez performed We Shall Overcome at the March.

comments.name: Keith
comments.body: I'd love to read her book. My father's cousin, Ann Romasco, nee Lockwood, worked at Highlander Center in eastern Tennessee during the civil rights movement. Highlander brought people together during the labor movement in the 1930s and civil rights movement two decades later to advocate for liberty. She became friends with Rosa Parks who wrote a beautiful letter in our family lore. Rosa Parks attended one of their workshops and returned to Birmingham determined not to take it anymore, and helped start the bus boycott. Miles Horton started the center with others and told me Rev. King liked to take credit for initiatives that were started by others like Rosa Parks. It's sad, but I'm not surprised, women who nourished many of activities were left in the shadows at that time.

comments.name: Grass Roots
comments.body:
As a native Montgomerian, I have a great interest in the book about these important women--but at the moment I have a "flighty" question: Why was Rosa Parks wearing gloves in August in DC? And they look like wool gloves, too? Would anyone know the answer? 

I recall, because I was a teenaged girl then, that women wore gloves and hats to important occasions. Jackie Kennedy had all those hats! 

Doesn't Mrs. Parks seem especially young and petite and vulnerable in the picture? The lifesized statue of her in downtown Montgomery reveals a surprisingly small figure--but look at her outsized influence!

comments.name: JoeG
comments.body: There's a famous photo of the March with Diahann Carroll, James Garner, and Paul  Newman. Ms. Carroll was a groundbreaker in her right.

comments.name: Cate
comments.body:
Yet another important and inspiring book to add to my growing library of works supportive of American women's historical significance.

This title, "How Bright the Path Grows..." is especially exciting as I was a junior in high school in August of 1963, just seventeen years old and, like so many American people, holding high our heads when looking at the "Negro" community's beautiful vision of the immediate need and demand for equal status and treatment. 

Even now, as a historian myself, I was not aware of much of the detail of the behind-the-scenes involvement, planning, and existential realities 
of the Civil Rights Movement, and in particular the history of so many of the women who made it all happen.

I'm placing my order for this important book as soon as I conclude my comment here. Looking forward to reading it!

comments.body: The reviews have been rather downbeat.

comments.name: fz
comments.body: I saw it in September. I love it. That music by Neko Case—!! The feelings the musical aroused in me had me imagining, hoping!, it will play forever. Not a soul that night who didn’t leap to their feet to applaud when it ended, so stirred.

comments.name: WN
comments.body: Every time I hear of another movie turned into a broadway size musical, I just shake my head.  It just feels like a creative cop out based on a tired formula.

comments.name: JJ Jones
comments.body: Back to the Future, the Original Sunset Blvd, Chitty Chitty Bang Bang all used cars effectively.  This creative team should rise to the challenge rather than avoiding it.

comments.name: sol hurok
comments.body:
So nuanced... Thelma and Louise is a terrific memorable film, but imagining it staged with no car and with music throughout - so that the plot and movement must pause over and over for songs - it kinda makes Me pause bigtime, as if I had to imagine what One Battle After Another would be like remade as a stage musical.  The rational answer should be NO!!  What a BAD IDEA!

The one and only element here that brings possibility to it is the inclusion of music by Neko Case, a fantastic, songwriter, singer, and musical artist.  But her participation still does not solve - in my mind - how Thelma and Louise can work as a stage musical.  A couple of years ago I was in the West End and went to see the Elvis Costello-scored stage musical of the great 1950s film drama A Face in the Crowd.  It was awful!  Every song - and there were way too many of them - sounded like an Elvis Costello song.  That shouldn't be a bad thing, but recognizing Elvis' clear style in those many frequent songs pulled me too far from the characters and action in the original film's solid story.  Requisite jack-in-the-box standing O at the end, and I had to wonder who ever saw the original film.

Maybe that's not the case for Thelma and Louise, but recreating that as a stage musical punctuated by Neko Case songs feels like a very similar recipe.  Too bad Ozzy died, he could have scored Psycho: The Musical.

comments.name: CHARLIE KATSU
comments.body: Sánchez sold out the courts to a runaway separatist to keep power and now that crew buried his housing scheme alive. The woman hauled out on a stretcher blamed him, yet he parades her like a trophy. One study found Catalonia's rent caps pushed about 10% of rentals off the market, so this freeze tells owners to run. A guy who rushed an amnesty drawing about 900,000 applications is the last man alive who should blame landlords.

comments.body: Someone who is a social housing/subsidised tenant in the city centre of one of the great cities has won at life.

comments.body: It was the right wing parties, Vox, PP and Junts, who rejected them, and with over 65% of Spaniards in favor of the consumer housing protective measures, there should be a political price to pay whenever elections happen.

comments.name: Gemilio
comments.body: A solution to the housing problem: rental prices adjusted yearly according to the Consumer Price Index. Maximum actual rent rent of 500 euros per bedroom per month. University students living away from home should be housed in subsidized university residences. A ban on tourist rentals—tourists should stay in hotels, where jobs are created

comments.name: Jack.
comments.body:
What is the rationale for not strictly curtailing short-term tourism rentals?  Fewer rentals, less tourism.  Problem solved.  De nada.

Wouldn't that also increase the supply of apartments for rent/sale in the immediate-to-short-term?  Another problem solved.  De nada. 

Can Sanchez's government not even garner enough support for these modest proposals?  His political career may have run its course.  Yes, time for new elections.   Adeu.

comments.name: Justin
comments.body:
Ending evictions and extending rental rate (i.e. price) controls would make the rental markets much worse than they already are.  

I have little sympathy for Maricarmen. She was a funcionario (a government employee) living in an apartment leased 75 years ago by her parents. She has a generous pension after a lifetime of guaranteed employment (the envy of most Spaniards). She had an offer to purchase the apartment at a 50% discounted rate, which she declined.  She refused several other offers of help. 

On the other hand, I have plenty of sympathy for young Spaniards trying to live independently and get their adult lives moving. Prices are crazy high, especially when you consider salaries are much lower here. The government has been stalling for years to reduce red tape (invented by the Spanish) and construct more apartments.

comments.name: JasonBradshaw
comments.body: Like everywhere else in Europe - and the US - the answer is to build more housing, not create unwieldy new regulations that don't work well when demand outstrips supply. The areas surrounding central Madrid have many areas where new housing can be built. That's what politicians should be encouraging - increase supply until it meets demand, which will cause rent rates to stabilize.

articles.title: Spanish Lawmakers Reject Eviction Freeze, Spurring Calls for Early Elections
articles.summary: The government had proposed more protections for tenants after outrage at the eviction of an 87-year-old woman in Madrid.

comments.name: Dana Thach
comments.body: Sexual Assault is a serious issue and shouldn’t be overlooked in any situation. In the Cornell sexual assault case, it is evident that Cornell—an ivy leauge school— failed to hold the seven men involved responsible for their actions and failed to protect one of their female students. Though, any situation or lawsuit will also always have two sides no matter how devastating the case is. It is frustrating to see that some students in the newsletter “Cornells Sexual Assault Case” with Sam Siftom speaking with Emma Goldberg made the remark that “Cornell was being unfairly singled out”. An absurd sexual assault case took place on their campus and following that they failed the victim. Beyond that, they are failing other victims of sexual assault, they are failing female students attending their school, and they ashamed the people of the nation. They deserve to be singled out, Cornell is a prestigious law school college that can’t even serve justice when they need to. Cornell and the seven men involved deserve no sympathy or protection for their future and reputation.

comments.name: Isla Polakoff
comments.body: The sexual assault case at Cornell is deeply disturbing, and reading about it altered my perspective on higher education. Beyond the tragedy, it lays the culture of misogyny. It feels as though institutional leadership is minimizing the gravity of the assault by raising questions about the 7 boys' futures—it is baffling that anyone could prioritize the prospects of the seven individuals involved over justice for an act of violence. This underlying misogyny is equally visible on social media. A divide emerged in how people responded: women overwhelmingly shared awareness about the case, while many men continued posting casually about sports and entertainment. This contrast exposes a troubling societal reality and raises essential questions about the values we instill in young women versus the lack of accountability and empathy we teach young men.

comments.name: Emily
comments.body: I honestly think that Cornell didn't do anything to even help Jane Doe at all and they haven't talked about her enough. It's disgusting to even think they made 5 of them write essays.  How is that supposed to let them understand that doing that isn't okay? Not sure if this guy was one of the people in the group chat but he didn't seem to care at all in the video going across social media right now.  There are a lot of comments on their pages everywhere and they just block the people instead of saying something. They already ruined their reputation so why not answer? They should have reacted better and did something about it and not waited until now that she spoke up. They have no chance of making the situation better or even apologizing.  They need to get the consequences they deserve.

comments.name: Lucia Popp
comments.body: The Cornell sexual assault case has taken over my social media and news platforms pover the last week. It is as if the only thing I am looking at is information relating to this case. I am disgusted by it. I see women all over the country speaking out about it, and most men choosing to look the other way. I do think that the major publicity that this case is receiving has made it easier for women to come out and acknowledge their own assault stories. My brother is in a fraternity at Cornell. This past week has been incredibly weird and in a way difficult for him. To hear that 7 frat brothers, and 50 others also involved that he most likely partied with or sat next to in class did something so unimaginable to a woman is horrifying and makes one rethink the institution they are a part of. This case is one of thousands; it is just one brought to the public eye. It illustrates the problems this country and the world are facing, the disrespect of women and the fear of men. I think it is so important that this has finally been revealed, I hope other victims find their voice because of it.

comments.name: Olivia R
comments.body: What happened was atrocious and the lack of action from the school and authorities disgusts me. While it hasn’t taken over my feed, it blowing up online isn’t surprising. Cornell is a big school and most big schools are likely to sweep things like this under the rug. When met with a lawsuit this big where Jane Doe is suing not only the men who did it to her but also the school for not taking action, news is quick to spread. The school's actions severely disappointed me. This isn’t a sexual assault case this is rape - Some people don’t know the difference but there is one - In this case this girl was raped. While it never should have happened Cornell should have stepped in as soon as they were made aware of this with more than just threats of expulsion, suspension, or the threat of writing numerous essays. Thinking that someone getting touched without their consent and traumatized is the equivalent to an essay is atrocious. In the future I’d like to go to college and have already heard of the things that could happen on campus. As a former victim I like to think I’m pretty knowledgeable on the difference between sexual assault, rape, and consent. People need to be held more accountable for these things no matter who they are or if they’re good at something. There are many cases where people seem more concerned for the perpetrator and their life because of the skills or opportunities they have without thinking about how this could impact the victim.

comments.name: Nola Voet
comments.body: Honestly it’s disgusting, nearly every day we hear about someone coming forward with a new claim of sexual assault, and nearly every day people dismiss it like a paint chip on their wall that they notice but don’t care enough about to do anything. As this disgusting case comes to light, we can hear people’s true points of view on not just the misogynistic tendencies of society, but also the way they act on these opinions. These people are trying to rationalize something that there should not be disagreement on whether it’s bad or not. It should not matter who the person assaulted is they should be believed and the assaulter should have a consequence more than just an essay or a slap on the wrist—these people need to be held accountable, especially in a place that is supposed to be safe. I personally think that this case and the lack of action from the school sheds light on the schools real beliefs and hopefully helps bring awareness to similar situations like these.

comments.name: Ye Myint Maung
comments.body:
Young students & families put their trust and funds into massive, elite institutions like Cornell for the benefit of education. Instead, they’ve received silence and lack of human remorse for the moral integrity of students and human beings. In the near-future, instead of putting faith in the next generations of leaders and inventors from prestigious universities, maybe we should first develop individuals with the courage to speak out for others and initiate the change that’s right.

For years, Cornell has attempted to silence this case in order to maintain their image as a prestigious university. Choosing your own reputation over an individual’s voice & rights is the kind of neglect that proves the lack of remorse over money & reputation many elite, universities are composed of.

comments.name: M
comments.location: Glenbard West HS Glen Ellyn, IL
comments.body: Firstly, I want to clarify that recent news about wanting to reveal the victim's identity is absolute insanity. Secondly, I want to elaborate on the situation on how Cornell is taking this, and how the only punishment towards the seven men was to write an essay. People online argue on how the punishment is idiotic and is nothing more than a joke for their disguising actions on the victim. Those seven men have to receive more than just a lousy essay, and be rightfully held accountable for their actions. From various news outlets, and stories on the internet, I’ve grown to understand that cases like these aren’t 100% justified and nothing is ever taken seriously. It sickens me that people who have done such horrific things are still going about their lives without any repercussions whatsoever. It morally makes me question society as a whole, and what they believe in.

articles.title: What Are You Thinking and Feeling About the Cornell Sexual Assault Case?
articles.summary: The fallout from a lawsuit brought by a woman who said she was raped on campus in 2024 has gripped the nation. What is your reaction to the news?

comments.name: Martic
comments.body: It's tough to write one great thriller/detective/police etc novel never mind a series. Even the greatest, e.g., Rex Stout and his Tecumseh Fox (vs Nero Wolf and Archie Goodwin) create a loser sometimes. Osman's first Thursday Murder Club book was good; the rest adequate.

comments.name: Flâneuse
comments.body: Perfect list. I love the spy stuff: glad to see Grisham taking one on.

comments.name: Julian
comments.body: I haven’t had social media since the beginning of August. This commitment to dissociate, strays far from my peers, however from a personal/mental standpoint I’ve never been better. Even before I moved away from social media, I was a firm believer of taking pictures with your eyes. In thirty years I would rather think back or be reminded of amazing moments in my life, if such a memory was engraved in my digital footprint I don’t believe it holds as much value. In order to fill the time I’ve taken back from social media I’ve started working out more, I got a job, and I get good grades. These are some of the insignificant things I’ve gained by simply deleting one or two apps off my phone, and after experiencing the benefits of online absence I can never go back.

comments.name: Jazlyn
comments.body: I use social media, but I don't post very often. I mainly post when I go on trips or come across beautiful sights and places I want to share with others. I usually post about once every two months, so it never really feels like an obligation. I enjoy sharing special moments and seeing my friends comments, but I don't feel the need to post about everything I do in my everyday life. For me, social media is more about sharing memorable experiences and beautiful moments than constantly updating people about my life.

comments.name: Adelyn F
comments.body: I think social media is a good way to share memories, but it can also have negative effects. I relate to the author because I sometimes want to post pictures when something exciting happens in my life. For example, if I go on vacation, go somewhere fun, or spend time with friends, I might want to take pictures and post them. One part of the article that stood out to me was when the author said, “Sharing makes it so, somehow.” I understand what she means because posting a picture can make a memory feel more important. When I look back at old pictures, I can remember what I was doing and who I was with. However, I do not think you have to post something for it to be a real memory. Some of my best memories are moments that I never posted online. Social media can also make people compare themselves to others. Someone might post pictures of a perfect vacation, expensive things, or a fun time with friends. It can make their life look better than it actually is. People usually post the best parts of their lives and not the bad or boring parts. Because of this, it is easy to forget that social media does not show everything. Overall, I think social media is useful for sharing memories and staying connected with people. I think it is important to enjoy experiences instead of always thinking about posting them. Sometimes putting your phone away and enjoying the moment makes the memory better.

comments.name: Nathalee
comments.body: Social media is something that the majority of people use. Social media’s so popular to the point that even my grandparents use it. Online platforms like instagram, facebook, Snapchat, etc. have users that post their “life” in it. In my case, I also share a lot. Most of the time, I post selfies, family pictures, food, and beautiful sceneries. In some cases, I advocate for issues that need to be seen and heard more. I put it in my story and share it as a post. Of course, not everything is meant to be shared online, so i only share the “good stuff” and keep the more personal things private, since a post in social media may result in conclusions from other people about a person's life.

I think it's important that we remind ourselves how much we already have. And that the people who post online only show their life the way they wish it was. And not the way it actually is.

comments.name: Emma Walti
comments.body: As a teenager, I do relate to Rachel Feintzig’s essay as she criticizes herself for feeling the need to post, as if it never happened if she does not. I always find myself reaching for my phone every time something funny or exciting happens to simply take a picture and post, “Look what happened, HaHaHa.” But it is not so simple because that one action can change the mood or vibe of whatever is going on. It is like sitting at a dinner table and someone having their phone faced up on the table, taking the occasional glance. While they may not be directly picking it up, texting, or scrolling, imagine the difference if that person had just left it in the car, a bag, or their pocket. The whole mood changes by just one thing—putting the phone away. There is no need to post or share what you are doing with the whole world or even some friends. Instead, be present, appreciate, and enjoy the little moments that do not last forever.

Was sorry though that the “How did it happen?” part of the piece’s lead-in questions really never got answered. Perhaps that level of info would be just too much to air in a publication with the NYT’s circulation. You could certainly trust ME with knowing the nuts and bolts of how to hack the FBI, but I’d imagine your legal dept. wouldn’t necessarily be OK with putting that info in the hands of someone with fewer moral scruples than I (or the average NYT reader). 

On the topic of “What can we do to protect ourselves?”, there was a great article here yesterday by Christopher Rowland, discussing how Epic Systems, the nation’s largest medical records vendor, has been having its own troubles with hackers. One takeaway: never click on any link purporting to be for a MyChart portal, only ever use the actual downloaded app. There’s at least some chance the email did not come from your medical provider, but is a phishing scam sent by a hacker.

Many East Asian countries depend at least partly on China for refined products like jet fuel, diesel and gasoline. They do not have enough of their own refineries to process crude oil for their needs.

These countries, like Australia and the Philippines, suffered a double blow last spring. Crude oil prices surged following the onset of the war in Iran. Then China drastically reduced exports of refined products to conserve supplies for its home market. The resulting shortage of refinery capacity meant that the extra cost of refining crude went through the roof at other suppliers, in addition to the cost of the crude oil itself.

Now countries in Asia are watching with concern as China begins curtailing exports of refined products again. But this time, crude oil prices are falling as more crude comes out of the Mideast. So the shock might not be quite as great.

What do you think other countries in Asia should do?

This could be achieved by levying excise taxes or special one-time fees to artificially raise pump prices for those who drive diesel pickup trucks and boats strictly for leisure and other recreational purposes, while simultaneously offering tax rebates or credits to commercial operators. Such a mitigating measure would discourage non-essential diesel consumption and insulate the broader economy from rising costs by confining the price shock to a smaller, wealthier upper-middle-class consumer segment purchasing high-end diesel trucks and boats for recreational purposes.

I have noticed the nonsensical, emotional rebuttal comments that amount to nothing more than “That’s not going to work, because, trust me, that’s not going to work,” or, “That won’t have a significant enough impact.” If this or another similar measure can bring down diesel prices even marginally for the broader economy, then it will be worth trying. Much of the first half of this article repeats findings we have already seen about LAFD’s staffing decisions and delayed evacuation warnings in Altadena. Independent confirmation matters, but what does this report add, and which recommendations will actually be implemented?

I also question the connection drawn between these communities and development driven by scarce affordable housing. Altadena dates to 1887. Its location against the foothills is hardly a recent response to California’s housing crisis. The risk is real, but that framing needs historical context.

The article could also examine what is already being done. Southern California Edison uses wildfire cameras, drones for inspections, public safety power shutoffs and grid upgrades. Those efforts do not settle questions of responsibility for the Eaton fire. They do raise an important question: where did existing safeguards fall short, and what would make them more effective?

California also requires insurance discounts for wildfire mitigation and provides temporary protections against wildfire-related nonrenewals in designated areas. How will this report affect insurance availability and premiums? Will residents receive meaningful credit for reducing risk?

Accountability matters. So does explaining what changes next, who will pay for those changes, and how they will protect people already living in these communities.
